title: Continuous Presence Practice
opening: Bring noticing into a routine activity that is already happening. Attend to sensory experience and thoughts; when attention wanders, notice that and return if it still fits the activity. Compare afterward with how you usually participate.

labels.figure: The optional attention cycle: choose a safe routine activity, notice sensory experience and thoughts, return after wandering when appropriate, then compare afterward.
labels.activity: What familiar, low-risk activity will you choose?
labels.noticing: What sensory detail or thought did you notice?
labels.wandering: Did attention wander? If so, what did you notice about that moment?
labels.return: Did you return to the activity, or choose another response?
labels.compare: How did this brief attempt compare with your usual participation?
labels.fit: Did noticing support the activity? What would make you pause or stop?
labels.private: This attempt is private to you. Save it only if you want a copy.
labels.sourceHint: Manuscript page 44; recovered source, authorship and adoption of every wording not independently established.
labels.sourceQuote: Choose a routine activity. Notice its sensory experience and your thoughts; return when attention wanders. At its end, compare the experience with your usual way of doing it.
labels.sourceAttribution: Supplied recovered manuscript, 82-page source edition, p. 44.
labels.sourceBoundary: This is an optional practice, not a rule for uninterrupted attention. A wandering thought can be useful and does not automatically invalidate the attempt. Keep attention on the surroundings when the activity needs it; do not force constant self-observation.

cases.name: Washing a cup
cases.before: A person usually washes a cup while planning the rest of the evening.
cases.after: For one low-risk wash, they notice warm water, the cup's weight and a recurring thought about a message. They return to washing, then compare the experience with their usual routine.
cases.reading: The point is the sequence of noticing, wandering and returning, followed by a comparison. The thought about the message may also matter; the practice does not require suppressing it or producing an insight.

cases.name: Crossing a busy street
cases.before: Someone considers tracking their breath while crossing.
cases.after: Traffic, signals and other people require their attention.
cases.reading: Do not turn inward when it competes with safe participation. External monitoring is primary here; choose another suitable time or skip the practice.

cases.name: Listening to a friend
cases.before: A listener notices thoughts arriving during a conversation.
cases.after: They can return attention to what the friend is saying without repeatedly checking whether they are focused.
cases.reading: Returning can be simple and brief. If self-monitoring starts to interrupt listening, drop the monitoring and attend to the conversation.
